module.title: 2 · IV as GMM
module.summary: Instrumental variables is GMM with the moment 'instruments are uncorrelated with the error.' We derive the IV/2SLS estimator from that single idea.

stages.title: The instrument moment condition
stages.html:
When a regressor is endogenous

In the model y = β₀ + β₁x + ε, OLS needs E[x·ε] = 0. If x is endogenous — correlated with ε through omitted variables, simultaneity, or measurement error — OLS is biased.

An instrument z is a variable that is (i) relevant — correlated with x — and (ii) exogenous — uncorrelated with the error. Exogeneity is exactly a moment condition:

E[ z · ε ] = E[ z · (y − β₀ − β₁x) ] = 0

Stacking the constant (its own instrument) and z, the moment function is

g(θ) = Z′ · (y − Xβ), where each row is zᵢ·(yᵢ − xᵢ′β)

The sample moment is ḡ(β) = (1/n) Z′(y − Xβ). This says: the residuals must be orthogonal to the instruments.

Key idea. IV is not a separate technique — it is GMM whose moment condition is "instruments are orthogonal to the error." OLS is the special case where the instruments are the regressors themselves (Z = X).

stages.title: Solving the just-identified case
stages.html:
One instrument per endogenous regressor

Suppose the number of instruments equals the number of parameters (m = k) — for one endogenous x with one instrument z, plus a constant. Then we can set the sample moment exactly to zero:

Z′(y − Xβ̂) = 0 ⟹ Z′Xβ̂ = Z′y ⟹ β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹ Z′y

That is the classic IV estimator. It is the just-identified GMM estimator, and because the system hits zero exactly, the weighting matrix W plays no role here.

Why it fixes endogeneity

Substitute y = Xβ + ε:

β̂ = β + (Z′X)⁻¹ Z′ε

As n grows, (1/n)Z′ε → E[z·ε] = 0 by the moment condition, so β̂ → β. The instrument's exogeneity is precisely what kills the bias term. Contrast OLS, where the analogous term is (X′X)⁻¹X′ε and (1/n)X′ε → E[x·ε] ≠ 0 when x is endogenous.

Relevance matters too. If z barely moves x, then Z′X ≈ 0 and (Z′X)⁻¹ explodes — a weak instrument. The estimator stays consistent but becomes wildly imprecise. Strength of instruments is the theme of the slider below.

stages.title: Endogeneity bias, then the IV fix
stages.note: We build a textbook endogenous case: x and ε share a common shock, so OLS is biased upward. The instrument z drives x but is independent of ε. Hand-rolled IV via the moment Z′(y−Xβ)=0 recovers the true slope β₁=2.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800

z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)            # instrument: relevant + exogenous
c = rng.normal(0, 1, n)            # common confounder
x = 0.8*z + c + rng.normal(0,1,n)  # x depends on z AND on confounder c
eps = c + rng.normal(0, 1, n)      # error shares c  -> x is endogenous
y = 1 + 2*x + eps                  # true beta1 = 2

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z])

b_ols = np.linalg.solve(X.T@X, X.T@y)
b_iv  = np.linalg.solve(Z.T@X, Z.T@y)   # (Z'X)^-1 Z'y = just-identified GMM

print(f'true beta1            = 2.000')
print(f'OLS  beta1 (biased)   = {b_ols[1]:.3f}')
print(f'IV   beta1 (GMM mom.) = {b_iv[1]:.3f}')
print(f'check moment Z′(y-Xb_iv) = {np.round(Z.T@(y - X@b_iv), 6)}  (≈ 0)')

stages.title: Same answer from statsmodels (the production tool)
stages.note: In practice you call statsmodels rather than hand-rolling. LinearIVGMM and IV2SLS give the same just-identified estimate as our moment solver. Note the positional API: LinearIVGMM(endog=y, exog=X, instrument=Z).
stages.code:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import LinearIVGMM, IV2SLS
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
z = rng.normal(0,1,n); c = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = 0.8*z + c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
eps = c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y = 1 + 2*x + eps
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z])

gmm = LinearIVGMM(y, X, Z).fit()
tsls = IV2SLS(y, X, Z).fit()
print('LinearIVGMM params:', np.round(gmm.params, 4))
print('IV2SLS      params:', np.round(tsls.params, 4))
print(f'\nGMM slope = {gmm.params[1]:.4f}   (true = 2.0)')

stages.title: Instrument strength vs. precision
stages.note: Slide the relevance coefficient (how strongly z drives x). Strong instruments give a tight, accurate IV slope; weak ones (near 0) leave the estimate noisy and unreliable even though it stays roughly centered on 2. The estimated slope and its SE are in the title.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import LinearIVGMM
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 600
z = rng.normal(0,1,n); c = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = {{relevance}}*z + c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
eps = c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y = 1 + 2*x + eps
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z])
m = LinearIVGMM(y, X, Z).fit()
b1, se1 = m.params[1], m.bse[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(z, x, s=10, color='#da9100', alpha=.4)
zz = np.linspace(z.min(), z.max(), 50)
plt.plot(zz, np.polyval(np.polyfit(z,x,1), zz), color='#6f6b57', lw=2)
plt.xlabel('instrument z'); plt.ylabel('regressor x')
plt.title(f'strength={{relevance}}  →  IV β1={b1:.2f}  SE={se1:.3f}')

stages.title: Check: which moment defines IV?
stages.prompt: What moment condition does instrumental-variables estimation impose to identify β?
stages.hint: OLS assumes the first one and fails when x is endogenous. IV replaces x with a variable assumed exogenous.
stages.explain: IV's identifying moment is E[z·ε] = 0: the instrument is uncorrelated with the error. (We also need E[z·x] ≠ 0 — relevance — but that is the opposite of choice 4.)

stages.title: Check: just-identified weighting
stages.prompt: In the just-identified IV case (one instrument per endogenous regressor), changing the GMM weighting matrix W:
choices: has no effect, because the sample moment is set exactly to zero
is required to make the estimator consistent
only matters if the errors are heteroskedastic
stages.hint: Think about the value of ḡ′Wḡ at the solution when ḡ can be driven to exactly 0.
stages.explain: When m = k, β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹Z′y makes ḡ(β̂) = 0 exactly, so ḡ′Wḡ = 0 for ANY W. The weighting matrix only matters once you are over-identified.

stages.title: Just-identified GMM has another name
stages.prompt: A just-identified GMM estimator (one moment per parameter, m = k) is numerically identical to the classic ___ estimator.
stages.lead: You just solved Z′(y − Xβ̂) = 0 exactly and recovered β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹Z′y — a name you already know.
stages.hint: It's the estimator from the previous unit that fixes endogeneity with an exogenous z.
stages.explain: The 'GMM is a brand-new method' trap: just-identified GMM = IV (and 2SLS in the linear case). The seductive belief is that GMM's machinery — the weight matrix W — always does something; but when m = k the moments hit zero exactly, so W cancels out and you get plain IV. Boundary: W only matters, and GMM only improves on IV, when you are over-identified (m > k) with extra valid moments. This is also why OLS and IV are GMM special cases, not rival methods.
